turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi. Nice to meet you too. 

Well, I came in because I just can't stop thinking about my face. Specifically, the left side of my face just looks... off. My nose and my jaw are crooked, and it's all I can see in every ID photo or whenever I have to turn my camera on for my online classes. 

People tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, but I know it's there. I feel like everyone in the CNC lab at work is staring at it, like they notice my face being messed up before they even notice my work. It's just constantly on my mind.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports a constant preoccupation with perceived facial defects (crooked nose and jaw) that others state they do not see.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe for certain that other people can see that something is wrong with your face?
turns.patient_response:
I mean, I don't know for absolute certain, because like I said, people tell me they don't see it. But... it's just so obvious. 

I feel like they have to be able to see it, and they're just being polite or, you know, they don't want to make me feel bad. When they look at me, I can just feel them noticing how crooked it is, even if they won't admit it to my face.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes a perceived physical defect involving their face being 'crooked' that other people state they do not see, consistent with preoccupation with a perceived appearance flaw.

turns.doctor_question: Do you think it’s possible that your face only seems crooked to you, even if it doesn’t actually look that way to other people?
turns.patient_response:
I mean... I guess theoretically it could be possible? But honestly, no. I really don't think so. 

When I look in the mirror or see a picture, it's just right there. It's not like a feeling or something I'm imagining, it's a physical thing on my face. So, even if people say they don't see it, I just... I can't believe it's only in my head. It's too real.

turns.doctor_question: Do you spend a lot of time checking your face in mirrors or photos?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do. A lot. Especially in the mornings before I leave for school. I just... I get stuck. 

I'll be in the bathroom checking the mirror, and then I use my phone camera to check it again. I end up fixing my hair over and over, or changing my shirt trying to find something that hides the angle better. I even ask my mom if it looks weird before I head out. 

Sometimes I do all that for so long that I actually miss my lab entirely. Or if I do make it in, I show up so wiped out from the whole routine that I can't even focus on what I'm doing.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors regarding appearance, including mirror checking, checking with a phone camera, excessive camouflaging (adjusting hair and clothes to hide angles), and reassurance seeking from their mother.

turns.doctor_question: If your face looked the way you wanted, would you still feel very anxious about being around other people?
turns.patient_response:
No, I really don't think so. If my face just looked normal... I wouldn't have any problem being around people. 

The whole reason I get so anxious in the first place is just because of how crooked it is, and knowing that people are seeing it. If that was fixed, I'm pretty sure I'd be completely fine going to class or work or whatever. I wouldn't have anything to hide anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes intense anxiety driven by the perceived defect of their face being 'crooked' and distress over other people seeing it.

turns.doctor_question: Apart from your concerns about your face, do you have any other beliefs that people are talking about you, watching you, or trying to harm you?
turns.patient_response:
No, nothing like that. I don't think anyone is trying to hurt me or secretly watching me or anything. 

Like I said, if I worry about people looking at me or talking about me, it's strictly just because I know they notice my face. But outside of that specific thing... no, I don't have any worries about people being out to get me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies persecutory beliefs, stating they do not believe anyone is watching them, trying to hurt them, or out to get them.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe with complete certainty that your face is actually deformed?
turns.patient_response:
I don't know if I'd use the word deformed with complete certainty. 

I mean, I know it looks really crooked and messed up to me. But... I guess sometimes I wonder if maybe it's not as extreme as I think it is. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm a hundred percent sure it's an actual deformity. I just know it looks wrong to me, and I hate it.
